names.official: Federal individual income tax (Internal Revenue Code §1 et seq.)

taxes.base: Taxable income of U.S. citizens and residents (worldwide) and U.S.-source income of non-residents: wages, business profits, interest, dividends, capital gains, retirement distributions.

rate.headline: 10% – 37% (seven brackets, made permanent in 2025)
details: Rates of 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35% and 37%; bracket thresholds differ by filing status and are indexed each year (Rev. Proc. 2025-32 for 2026).
2026 standard deduction: $16,100 single; $32,200 married filing jointly; $24,150 head of household.
Long-term capital gains and qualified dividends are taxed separately at 0%, 15% or 20%, plus a 3.8% net investment income tax for higher incomes.

instruments.explanation: The largest federal revenue source. The One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (July 2025) made the 2017 rate structure permanent instead of letting it expire at the end of 2025.
exceptions: Most states also tax income; the federal tax is separate and additional.
Many credits, deductions and phase-outs change the amount actually owed.

names.official: Federal corporate income tax (Internal Revenue Code §11)

taxes.base: Taxable income of corporations organised in the United States (worldwide income, with foreign tax credits) and U.S.-source income of foreign corporations.

rate.headline: 21% flat
details: Flat 21% rate on taxable income since 2018.
A 15% corporate alternative minimum tax applies to very large corporations (over $1 billion of average financial-statement income).

instruments.explanation: A single-rate tax on corporate profits. Revenue fluctuates with profits and with depreciation rules, which the 2025 legislation loosened.
exceptions: Pass-through businesses (partnerships, S corporations, sole proprietorships) are taxed under the individual income tax instead.
State corporate taxes are additional.

names.official: Old-Age, Survivors and Disability Insurance payroll taxes (FICA and SECA)

taxes.base: Wages and self-employment earnings up to the annual contribution and benefit base ($184,500 in 2026).
taxes.payer: Employees and employers (6.2% each); self-employed pay 12.4%.

rate.headline: 6.2% employee + 6.2% employer (12.4% combined), up to $184,500 (2026)
details: Self-Employment Contributions Act (SECA) rate is 12.4% for OASDI.
Only earnings up to the wage base are taxed.

instruments.explanation: A contribution credited to the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Disability Insurance trust funds, which pay Social Security benefits. Legally an excise/payroll tax, but earmarked and tied to benefit entitlement.
exceptions: Some state and local government employees are outside Social Security.
Railroad workers have a separate system (Railroad Retirement Tax Act).

names.official: Hospital Insurance (Medicare Part A) payroll taxes (FICA and SECA)

taxes.base: All wages and self-employment earnings, with no wage cap.
taxes.payer: Employees and employers (1.45% each); self-employed pay 2.9%; higher earners pay an additional 0.9%.

rate.headline: 1.45% employee + 1.45% employer (2.9%), plus 0.9% above $200,000
details: Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% on earnings above $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (joint), paid by the employee only.
A separate 3.8% net investment income tax is collected through the individual income tax.

instruments.explanation: A contribution credited to the Hospital Insurance trust fund that pays for Medicare Part A.
exceptions: Medicare Parts B and D are financed mainly by general revenue and premiums, not this tax.

names.official: Unemployment insurance taxes (Federal Unemployment Tax Act and state unemployment taxes deposited to the Unemployment Trust Fund)

taxes.base: Employers' payroll up to a wage base ($7,000 federal; states set higher bases).
taxes.payer: Employers (in a few states also employees).

rate.headline: Federal 6.0% (0.6% after state-credit); state rates vary by employer
details: FUTA: 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each worker's wages, with a credit of up to 5.4% for state contributions, leaving 0.6% in most states.
State unemployment taxes: each state sets wage bases and experience-rated rates for each employer.

instruments.explanation: Financing for unemployment benefits. Most receipts in the Treasury statement are state taxes deposited into the federal Unemployment Trust Fund, so this core mixes one federal and fifty state programmes.
exceptions: State rates change annually with each employer's layoff experience and the trust-fund balance.

names.official: Federal excise taxes (fuels, tobacco, alcohol, air transportation, trucks and other)

taxes.base: Specific goods and activities: motor fuels, tobacco, alcohol, air tickets and cargo, heavy trucks, health-insurance-related fees and others.
taxes.payer: Producers, importers or sellers; passed on to consumers.

rate.headline: Specific and ad valorem rates by product
details: Gasoline 18.4¢ and diesel 24.4¢ per gallon; cigarettes about $1.01 per pack; air passenger tickets 7.5% (domestic).
Several excise taxes fund trust funds (Highway, Airport and Airway, Black Lung).

instruments.explanation: Taxes on specific products. Many rates are fixed in dollars and are not indexed to inflation, so their revenue share has declined over decades.
exceptions: The list of taxed items is long; see Subtitle D of the Internal Revenue Code.

legalRefs.locator: 26 U.S.C. Subtitle D and E, e.g. §4081 (fuels), §5701 (tobacco), §5001 (spirits), §4261 (air transportation)

names.official: Federal estate and gift taxes (Internal Revenue Code Chapters 11–12)

taxes.base: Value of large estates at death and of large lifetime gifts above the exclusion.

rate.headline: 40% top rate above a $15 million exclusion (2026)
details: The basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 per person from 2026 (permanent, indexed after 2026).
Amounts above the exclusion are taxed on a graduated scale reaching 40%.

instruments.explanation: A wealth-transfer tax paid by very few estates.
exceptions: Transfers to a spouse and to charities are deductible; some states levy their own estate or inheritance taxes.

instruments.statusNote: The IEEPA tariffs behind the FY2025 increase were ended on 24 February 2026 after the Supreme Court's ruling of 20 February 2026 (Learning Resources v. Trump). A temporary Section 122 surcharge (24 Feb–24 Jul 2026) was replaced in late July 2026 by Section 301 'forced-labour' duties of 10% or 12.5% on 60 economies; Section 232 sectoral tariffs continue. Refunds of IEEPA duties are being litigated.

names.official: Customs duties and import tariffs (Tariff Act; Harmonized Tariff Schedule; Sections 122, 232, 301)

taxes.base: Value of imported goods by tariff classification and origin.
taxes.payer: Importers of record; passed on in prices.

rate.headline: HTSUS rates plus changing additional tariffs (Sections 232, 301 and others)
details: Baseline (MFN) rates are set line by line in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule and are mostly low.
IEEPA tariffs: terminated 24 Feb 2026 after the Supreme Court held IEEPA does not authorise tariffs.
Section 301 forced-labour action (July 2026): 10% for economies that ban or commit to ban forced-labour imports, 12.5% for the rest, covering 60 economies.
Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminium and other sectors and earlier Section 301 tariffs on China are separate authorities.

instruments.explanation: Duties collected at the border by Customs and Border Protection. Revenue jumped from $77 billion in FY2024 to $195 billion in FY2025 as additional tariffs took effect; the legal basis and level of those tariffs have changed repeatedly in 2026.
exceptions: Trade agreements, exclusions and product-specific orders change the applicable rate; check the HTSUS and CBP notices.

names.official: State individual income taxes

taxes.base: Income of residents (and non-residents' in-state income) as defined by each state, usually starting from federal adjusted gross income.

rate.headline: Varies by state – 41 states plus DC tax broad income; about 2.5% to 13.3% top rates
details: Eight states levy no broad-based income tax (AK, FL, NV, NH, SD, TN, TX, WY).
About 15 states use a single flat rate; the others use graduated brackets, with California's top rate at 13.3%.

instruments.explanation: The largest state tax by revenue after sales taxes, and the one that varies most between states.
exceptions: Washington taxes capital gains only; some states tax only interest, dividends or specific income.

names.official: State general sales and use taxes

taxes.base: Retail sales of tangible goods and, in many states, some services; use tax on items bought out of state.

rate.headline: Varies by state – 45 states plus DC levy one; state rates from 2.9% to 7.25%
details: Five states (AK, DE, MT, NH, OR) have no state sales tax; Alaska allows local ones.
Local sales taxes add to the state rate; combined rates can exceed 10%.

instruments.explanation: A tax on retail purchases. Since South Dakota v. Wayfair (2018), states can require remote sellers with enough economic activity to collect the tax.
exceptions: Food, medicine and services are exempt or taxed at lower rates in many states.

names.official: State corporation net income and franchise taxes

taxes.base: Net income of corporations apportioned to the state (Census category T41).

rate.headline: Varies by state – flat and graduated rates; some states use gross-receipts taxes instead
details: Most states levy a corporate income tax; a few (e.g. Nevada, Texas, Washington) use gross-receipts or similar taxes instead.

instruments.explanation: State taxes on business profits, apportioned by each state's own formula.
exceptions: Not every state has one; gross-receipts taxes are not counted in this Census category.

names.official: State motor fuels taxes

taxes.base: Gallons of gasoline, diesel and other motor fuels.

rate.headline: Varies by state – cents per gallon, some indexed
details: Each state sets its own per-gallon rates, and some adjust them with inflation or fuel prices.

instruments.explanation: Fuel taxes that mostly finance roads. Federal fuel excise taxes (18.4¢ gasoline) are additional.
exceptions: Electric-vehicle registration fees are increasingly used to replace lost fuel-tax revenue.

names.official: State selective sales taxes: alcohol, tobacco, insurance premiums, utilities, amusements, sports betting and other

taxes.base: Specific products and activities (Census items T10–T12, T15, T16, T18 and T19).

rate.headline: Varies by state and product
details: Includes tobacco, alcohol, insurance premium taxes (a large item), public-utility taxes, amusement and gambling taxes, sports-betting taxes and taxes on cannabis and other products.

instruments.explanation: Product-specific taxes that sit beside the general sales tax. Motor fuels are shown in their own core.
exceptions: The category 'other selective sales' includes taxes on cannabis, sugary drinks and similar items.

names.official: State property taxes

taxes.base: Assessed value of property where a state itself levies a tax (Census item T01 for states).

rate.headline: Varies by state – most property tax is local
details: Only a few states levy a state-level property tax; local governments collect the vast majority of property taxes.

instruments.explanation: A small state-level item; property tax is mostly a local tax in the United States.
exceptions: Some states levy statewide school property taxes that appear as state revenue.

names.official: State license taxes (motor vehicle, corporate, occupation and business, hunting and fishing and other)

taxes.base: Permission to own a vehicle, operate a business or profession, or hunt and fish (Census items T20–T29).

rate.headline: Varies by state and licence type
details: Motor vehicle registration and licence taxes are the largest part.

instruments.explanation: Charges for licences and permits that the Census Bureau counts as taxes.
exceptions: Some are set to recover administrative cost; others are revenue-raising.

names.official: State severance taxes on oil, gas, coal and minerals

taxes.base: Value or volume of natural resources extracted within the state.

rate.headline: Varies by state and resource
details: Rates are percentages of value or per-unit amounts and differ widely; oil-producing states rely on them heavily.

instruments.explanation: Taxes on extracting natural resources. Royalties paid to states for their own lands are non-tax revenue and are not included.
exceptions: Rates often depend on well type, price and production level.

names.official: Other state taxes: death and gift, documentary and stock transfer, and other

taxes.base: Estates, property transfers and other taxes not classified elsewhere (Census items T50, T51 and T99).

rate.headline: Varies by state
details: Several states levy estate or inheritance taxes; many charge real-estate transfer (documentary) taxes.

instruments.explanation: A miscellaneous group of smaller state taxes.
exceptions: Exemption thresholds for state estate taxes are far lower than the federal $15 million.

legalRefs.locator: New York real estate transfer tax example

names.official: Local property taxes (counties, municipalities, townships, school districts and special districts)

taxes.base: Assessed value of land and buildings (and in some places business personal property).

rate.headline: Varies by jurisdiction – millage set by each taxing unit
details: Each county, city, school district and special district sets its own rate; a parcel's bill combines several.
Many states cap rate or assessment growth (for example California's Proposition 13).

instruments.explanation: The main local tax. School districts alone raise about 45% of it (Census, FY2024).
exceptions: Homestead exemptions and caps vary; some states equalise school funding across districts.

names.official: Local general sales and use taxes

taxes.base: Retail sales within the city, county or district, usually on the same base as the state tax.

rate.headline: Varies by locality – from a fraction of a percent to about 5%
details: Authorised by state law; about 38 states permit local sales taxes.
The combined state-and-local rate is what the customer pays.

instruments.explanation: Local add-ons to the state sales tax, used by cities, counties and transit or special districts.
exceptions: Some states (e.g. Louisiana, Colorado) have many overlapping local rates and separate local administrations.

names.official: Local individual and corporation income and wage taxes

taxes.base: Wages, net profits and (in a few places) corporate income within the locality.

rate.headline: Varies by locality – levied in a minority of states
details: Allowed in a minority of states, including Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Kentucky, Maryland, Indiana and New York (New York City).

instruments.explanation: Municipal earnings taxes and county income taxes. Many cities tax people who work there but live elsewhere.
exceptions: Rates and bases differ, and Ohio municipalities can coordinate through state-set rules.

names.official: Local selective sales and gross receipts taxes (utilities, hotels, motor fuel, amusements and others)

taxes.base: Specific services and products such as public utilities, lodging, entertainment and tobacco (Census items T10–T19).

rate.headline: Varies by locality
details: Utility gross-receipts taxes and lodging (hotel) taxes are the largest parts.

instruments.explanation: Local taxes on particular services rather than all retail sales.
exceptions: Only some states allow them.

legalRefs.locator: Definition of items T10–T19 (also used for local governments)

names.official: Local license taxes and business licence charges

taxes.base: Business licences, occupation and other permits classified by the Census Bureau as license taxes.

rate.headline: Varies by locality
details: Set by ordinance under state law.

instruments.explanation: Charges for the right to do business or hold a licence.
exceptions: Some are revenue taxes on gross receipts rather than flat fees.

names.official: Other local taxes: documentary and transfer taxes, death and gift, severance and other

taxes.base: Real-estate transfers and other taxes not classified elsewhere (Census items T50, T51, T53, T99).

rate.headline: Varies by locality
details: Some cities (e.g. New York City, Philadelphia) levy their own real-estate transfer taxes.

instruments.explanation: A residual category of smaller local taxes.
exceptions: Not available in every state.

legalRefs.locator: New York example (state and city transfer taxes)
